title: The Petrodollar is Dying. Nobody is Announcing it.
author: Anhad Singh
excerpt: A deep dive into the 1974 US-Saudi handshake, the weaponization of the dollar, and the shift toward a multipolar energy economy.
content:
In 1974, the United States and Saudi Arabia made a deal that changed the world. America would provide military protection and weapons to the Kingdom. In return, Saudi Arabia would price its oil exclusively in US dollars and invest its extra money in American Treasury bonds. This arrangement was not a treaty and did not go through Congress. It was a handshake between two governments that understood their exchange clearly. Other OPEC nations followed suit. Just like that, the dollar became the standard in global energy.

To understand why this matters, you need to see what it created. Every country needed oil. Therefore, every country needed dollars. This meant every country had to hold dollars in reserve. As a result, America could print money, run deficits, and fund wars in a way no other country could because the demand for its currency was guaranteed. This demand was driven not just by the strength of its economy but also by the price of crude oil.

But before Saudi Arabia, there was Iran.

In the decades before 1979, Iran under the Shah was one of America’s key allies in the Middle East. American and British oil companies had deep ties to Iran's oil infrastructure going back to the early 20th century. The 1953 coup, led by the CIA and British intelligence, restored the Shah after Prime Minister Mosaddegh tried to nationalise Iranian oil. America was not protecting democracy; it was securing access to Iranian oil. The Shah maintained oil production while Washington supported his regime. It was a smooth arrangement until it wasn’t.

The 1979 revolution changed everything. Ayatollah Khomeini’s government expelled the Americans, took hostages, and made confrontation with Washington central to its ideology. America responded with sanctions that have just been lifted by Trump as a cry for help. Over the past four decades, Iran has been mostly cut off from the dollar system, which is like being cut off from the global economy. In this isolation, Iran did something most sanctioned countries do not do. It prepared.

This is where the Strait of Hormuz comes in.

Twenty percent of the world’s oil passes through this waterway, which is only 33 Km wide at its narrowest point. Iran sits on one side. The entire global energy supply chain runs through it. For years, this was a theoretical issue. Last year, it became real. Iranian proxies and direct attacks brought the world closer to a closure of Hormuz than it had been in decades. Shipping costs soared. Insurance premiums for vessels in the Gulf became nearly unbearable. The world got a glimpse of what Iran had been building quietly for twenty years: coordinated pressure, asymmetric capability, and a willingness to endure hardship for leverage.

Now Khamenei is dead. The next leader is not likely to seek diplomacy. Iran has seen America impose sanctions, assassinate its generals, sabotage its nuclear facilities, and support all its regional foes. The new leadership doesn’t need to create anger. It has two decades worth already built up.

Trump’s return to maximum pressure has not stabilised the situation. He made it worse. Threatening to bomb Iran’s oil infrastructure may sound like a deterrent, but Iran’s response to an existential threat has never been retreat. Instead, it is likely to escalate through every proxy and chokepoint it has developed over twenty years. Professor Jiang Xueqin and others modeling this situation agree. A ground invasion or direct attack on Iran won’t end the conflict, it will spark a regional unraveling that the fragile global economy, weakened by AI speculation, rising debt, and post-pandemic issues, is not ready to handle.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia quietly allowed its petrodollar agreement with America to expire last year. There was no announcement. The deal simply lapsed. Riyadh is now selling oil to China in yuan. It is balancing its relationships, keeping one foot in Washington and one in Beijing. It has seen Iran suffer from reliance on one side and intends to avoid that mistake.

Gold purchases by central banks reached record levels in 2022 and 2023. China, Russia, India, and several emerging economies are accumulating gold with unusual urgency. The reason is straightforward. When America froze Russia’s dollar reserves after Ukraine, every government that was not a close American ally got the same message. Dollar reserves are not neutral; they are a weapon. Gold is not.

The petrodollar is not collapsing tomorrow. The dollar still holds dominance. However, the foundations that guaranteed that dominance, including the Saudi deal, Iranian compliance, and the steady American naval presence in the Gulf, are slowly breaking apart. The system is not ending with a declaration. It is ending as most things do: slowly, then all at once.

title: Weaponising Energy: How the Strait of Hormuz Became the Epicentre for Economic Warfare
author: Anhad Singh
excerpt: An exploration of the Strait of Hormuz as a strategic 'kill button' for global energy and the shift toward a multipolar world order.
content:
"Whoever controls the flow of energy controls the future of the nations".

The Strait of Hormuz has become a household name by this point of time in the world. But why is it so important? Why does Iran control it? What is its relation to global markets, world economies and energy resources? Well the simple answer in layman terms is that it's a global chokepoint that Iran has taken control over, whereas after doing deeper research I have found that it is not just a chokepoint, its the kill button, and Iran has strategically got its index on it.

Allow me to share with you some background information. One-Fifth of the world's oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Along with that China signed a 25 year agreement in 2021 that China will invest $400 billion in Iran’s economy in exchange for a steady and heavily discounted supply of oil from Iran. Under this agreement China gets a minimum guaranteed discount of 12% on oil prices, plus an additional 6-8% discount for risk.

THE PROVOCATION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING

Now, this didn't happen in a vacuum. Trump's administration, along with Netanyahu and Israel, had been escalating tensions with Iran for years. When Trump withdrew from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018, he imposed what they called "maximum pressure" sanctions on Iran. This wasn't just diplomacy it was economic warfare. Israel, backed by Trump, launched strikes and conducted covert operations against Iranian nuclear facilities. These weren't subtle moves. They were deliberate provocations designed to destabilize Iran.

But here's where it gets interesting. Instead of backing down, Iran made a calculated strategic move. They realized that the Western world was trying to suffocate their economy through sanctions. So what did they do? They turned to China. They deepened their alliance and locked in that 25 year deal. It wasn't just about survival it was about flipping the script. Iran understood that if they couldn't compete in the Western-dominated global economy, they would become indispensable to the rising power of the East. China needed oil. Iran had oil. And most importantly, Iran controlled the Strait of Hormuz.

This was Iran's answer to Trump and Netanyahu's aggression. This was Iran saying: "You want to play economic warfare? Fine. But remember, 20% of the world's oil comes through my waters."

WHO ACTUALLY OWNS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ?

Here's where international law gets interesting, and frankly, where most people get it wrong. Iran doesn't actually own the Strait of Hormuz outright. According to international maritime law, specifically the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), every country has the right to claim territorial waters extending 12 nautical miles (roughly 22 kilometers) from its coastline.

The Strait of Hormuz is about 33 nautical miles wide at its narrowest point. This means that both Iran and Oman have territorial waters within the strait. Iran controls the southern half, while Oman controls the northern half. Technically, large portions of the strait are international waters, and ships have the "right of innocent passage".

But here's the catch: the sea on the side of Oman is unstable, it has terrible turbulence which do not allow ships to pass through it. Whereas Iran sits on the southern shore of the strait, its waters are calm and allow ships to pass through, it also controls the islands within it, and has military capabilities that can reach into those international waters. It's not ownership in the legal sense, but it's control in the practical sense.

THE PETRODOLLAR AND ITS DECLINING POWER

For decades, the United States maintained its global dominance through a simple but brilliant mechanism: oil is traded in US dollars. This meant that every country needed dollars to buy oil. This gave America enormous power. It allowed them to print money, to run massive deficits, and to sanction countries at will. It was the backbone of American economic dominance.

But this system is crumbling. When China and Iran trade oil now, they're increasingly doing it in Chinese yuan instead of US dollars. This is revolutionary. It means China doesn't need dollars to buy Iranian oil. It means Iran can access revenue without going through the dollar system. It's a direct challenge to American economic dominance.

THE TWO MILLION DOLLAR TOLL AND TRUMP'S BLOCKADE

Iran proposed a toll system: a fee that every ship passing through the Strait of Hormuz would have to pay. We're talking about 2 million dollars per vessel. Trump blocked it because if Iran successfully implemented a toll system, it would be a public admission that Iran controls the strait. It would shatter the myth of American power.

This is economic warfare in its purest form. Trump and the West were trying to suffocate Iran's economy through sanctions. Iran was trying to leverage its geographic position to extract wealth from global commerce. As a result trump stated that he would essentially block the blockade done by Iran, which was later proved substantial when the US navy allowed Chinese ships to pass through.

THE BIGGER PICTURE

What we're witnessing with the Strait of Hormuz isn't just a regional conflict. It's a larger shift happening in global geopolitics. The unipolar American world order is declining. The petrodollar is weakening. China is rising. And Iran, despite being sanctioned and isolated, has managed to position itself as a critical player in this new world order.

Iran didn't start this conflict. Trump and Netanyahu did, with their aggressive policies and military provocations. But Iran responded intelligently. They didn't try to compete with America on America's terms. Instead, they moved to a different playing field entirely.

The Strait of Hormuz has become the epicentre of economic warfare because energy is power, and whoever controls energy controls the future of nations.

title: The New Oil Is Not Data. It's Electricity.
author: Anhad Singh
excerpt: AI may define this decade, but the bottleneck is not software — it is power. Why utilities, grids, and energy infrastructure may be the asymmetric trade.
content:
Every cycle has a phrase that becomes so overused it loses all meaning.

In the 2000s it was globalization.

In the 2010s it was data.

Today it is AI.

The problem with investment manias is not that they are wrong. The problem is that they are often directionally right and financially disastrous at the same time.

The internet changed the world. Most internet stocks still got obliterated.

Railroads transformed America. Most railroad investors went bankrupt.

AI will likely be the defining technology of this decade. That does not automatically mean AI companies will be the defining investments.

Investors are asking the wrong question.

The question is not who builds the best model.

The question is what becomes scarce if AI succeeds.

History offers a useful framework.

When automobiles emerged, the winning trade was not necessarily car manufacturers. Hundreds of them disappeared. The more durable winners were the businesses that enabled an automotive society. Oil companies, tire manufacturers, road construction firms, insurance providers, and suburban real estate all became beneficiaries of a structural shift.

Technological revolutions rarely reward the obvious participants. They reward the bottlenecks.

Today, the bottleneck is electricity.

Every major AI model ultimately reduces to one thing: massive computational power. Computational power requires data centers. Data centers require energy. Lots of it.

For the better part of two decades, developed economies operated under the assumption that electricity demand would remain relatively flat. Efficiency improvements offset incremental consumption. Energy became a utility rather than a growth industry.

That assumption is now breaking.

The average large AI training run consumes exponentially more power than traditional software workloads. Hyperscalers are investing hundreds of billions of dollars into infrastructure that requires a physical backbone. Unlike software, electrons cannot be scaled through clever code.

They must be generated.

This creates a fascinating investment setup.

Markets have spent the last three years obsessing over AI applications while largely ignoring the industries required to sustain them.

Utilities, power transmission networks, grid modernization companies, natural gas infrastructure, nuclear developers, and industrial equipment manufacturers suddenly find themselves at the center of the most important technological trend of our generation.

This is not a temporary phenomenon.

Civilizations are ultimately constrained by energy.

Economic growth is simply humanity's ability to consume more energy and direct it toward increasingly productive outcomes.

The Industrial Revolution was an energy story.

The rise of America was an energy story.

China's manufacturing dominance was an energy story.

AI is becoming an energy story.

The market's fixation on software obscures a deeper reality. Every technological leap eventually collides with physical limits.

Cloud computing required data centers.

E-commerce required logistics networks.

Streaming required broadband infrastructure.

AI requires power.

The most interesting opportunities often emerge where narratives and fundamentals diverge.

Narratives currently favor software.

Fundamentals increasingly favor infrastructure.

This does not mean AI companies are poor investments. Some will become enormously valuable. But markets have a tendency to crowd into obvious stories while neglecting the second-order consequences.

Second-order effects are where asymmetric returns usually live.

Investors should ask themselves a simple question.

If AI adoption doubles over the next five years, who benefits regardless of which model wins?

The answer is unlikely to be found in another chatbot.

It might be found in the companies ensuring the lights stay on.

For decades, energy was viewed as a legacy industry.

The next decade may prove it was merely sleeping.

And if history is any guide, the biggest fortunes are often made by identifying the bottleneck before everyone else realizes it exists.

title: The Middle East Ceasefire Changes Less Than People Think
author: Anhad Singh
excerpt: Markets love events. History loves structures. Why the Iran–Israel ceasefire is a pause — not a resolution — in the contest for regional order.
content:
Markets love events.

History loves structures.

The difference between the two explains why investors and policymakers consistently misunderstand geopolitics.

The recent ceasefire between Iran and Israel has been interpreted as a turning point. Commentators are already debating winners and losers. Some see de-escalation. Others see deterrence restored. A few believe the region has stepped back from the brink.

They may all be missing the larger picture.

The ceasefire is important.

The forces that produced the conflict are far more important.

To understand what happens next, it is necessary to understand what actually changed and what remained exactly the same.

For decades, the Middle East operated under a relatively stable strategic framework. America acted as the primary security guarantor. Regional powers competed, but largely within boundaries enforced by overwhelming US military dominance.

That order has been gradually eroding.

The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan weakened American appetite for large-scale intervention. China's economic rise shifted Washington's strategic focus toward Asia. Regional actors increasingly recognized that they would need to navigate a world with less direct American involvement.

This created a vacuum.

Vacuums rarely stay empty.

Iran expanded its network of proxies across the region. Saudi Arabia pursued a more independent foreign policy. Turkey became increasingly assertive. Israel faced a growing number of security challenges that no longer fit traditional military frameworks.

The recent conflict emerged from this changing landscape.

Many observers frame the confrontation as a military dispute.

It is better understood as a contest over regional order.

The central question is not who won a particular exchange.

The central question is who gets to shape the Middle East after the American unipolar moment.

That question remains unanswered.

The ceasefire therefore represents a pause rather than a resolution.

History offers numerous examples.

The Korean War ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

The Cold War experienced repeated periods of de-escalation without resolving its underlying rivalry.

India and Pakistan have repeatedly stepped back from escalation while preserving the structural conditions that make future crises possible.

Ceasefires stop violence.

They rarely eliminate incentives.

Those incentives remain firmly in place today.

Iran still seeks strategic depth.

Israel still seeks security guarantees.

Arab states still seek stability without becoming dependent on any single external power.

The United States still wants regional influence while reducing regional commitments.

China still wants economic access without security responsibilities.

None of these objectives disappeared because of a ceasefire.

The economic implications are equally significant.

The global economy has become remarkably dependent on a small number of geopolitical chokepoints.

The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most strategically important waterways in the world. A substantial portion of global energy flows through a region where miscalculation can occur within hours.

Markets periodically forget this reality.

Then a crisis emerges and everyone remembers.

The broader lesson is that globalization is evolving rather than disappearing.

The era of frictionless globalization was built upon assumptions of stability.

Those assumptions are increasingly being challenged.

Supply chains are becoming strategic assets.

Energy security is becoming national security.

Industrial policy is returning after decades of neglect.

Governments are prioritizing resilience alongside efficiency.

The Middle East sits at the center of these shifts.

What happens there no longer stays there.

A missile strike can affect energy prices in Europe.

A shipping disruption can impact manufacturing in Asia.

A regional escalation can influence inflation expectations in the United States.

Geopolitics has become a macroeconomic variable again.

For much of the post-Cold War era, investors could largely ignore it.

That luxury is disappearing.

The most likely outcome is neither permanent peace nor immediate war.

It is prolonged competition under a fragile equilibrium.

Periods of calm will alternate with periods of confrontation.

Markets will repeatedly mistake temporary stabilization for permanent resolution.

They always do.

The deeper story is not the ceasefire itself.

The deeper story is the transition from one global order to another.

The post-1991 world was defined by overwhelming American dominance.

The next world will likely be defined by multiple centers of power, overlapping spheres of influence, and constant negotiation between competing interests.

The Middle East is not separate from that transition.

It is one of the places where that transition is being tested in real time.

That is why the ceasefire matters.

Not because it ended a conflict.

But because it revealed the shape of the conflicts still to come.

title: The Iran War: What the News Is Not Telling You
author: Anhad Singh
excerpt: The ceasefire is paper. The war is ongoing. The full account of February 28, Hormuz, Lebanon, and why nothing is resolved.
content:
The full, unfiltered account of how a war started, who is really running it, what a ceasefire actually means, and why nothing is resolved

PART I: STOP. THIS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK IT IS.

Every news channel is covering the Iran situation. Almost none of them are telling you the complete picture.

Here is what the average person consuming mainstream media believes: America and Israel struck Iran because of nuclear concerns. A war was fought. A ceasefire was reached. A deal is being negotiated. The Strait of Hormuz is opening. Crisis over.

Here is what is actually happening.

A war that began on February 28, 2026 has killed thousands of people, displaced over a million in Lebanon alone, sent global oil prices to levels not seen since the 1970s, and triggered what the International Energy Agency officially called "the greatest global energy security challenge in history." The ceasefire signed on June 17 is being violated as you read these words. The US struck Iranian targets again on June 26. Iran fired drones at a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz on June 26 in what Trump confirmed was a ceasefire violation. Israel is conducting active military operations in Lebanon that both Iran and Lebanon's own government have called war crimes. And the nuclear question, the stated reason for all of this, remains completely unresolved.

The deal is paper. The war is ongoing. And the story behind the story goes back decades.

PART II: THE ROAD TO FEBRUARY 28 — EVERYTHING THAT CAME BEFORE

To understand what happened on February 28, 2026, you need to understand the architecture of pressure that was built over years to make that date inevitable.

It begins in 1979. The Iranian Revolution ended America's deepest alliance in the Middle East, an alliance that had been reconstructed by the CIA in 1953 when Operation Ajax overthrew Mohammad Mosaddegh, the democratically elected Prime Minister who had nationalized Iranian oil. America reinstalled the Shah. The Shah ruled through SAVAK, one of the most brutal secret police forces of the 20th century. When the revolution finally came, its fury was directed not just at the Shah but at America, which had kept the Shah in power for 26 years after stealing the country's democracy.

This is the origin of the hostility. Not Iranian irrationality. Not Islamic extremism. A direct, documented consequence of American interference in Iranian sovereignty.

From 1979 onward, the United States constructed an architecture of maximum pressure around Iran. Sanctions that over decades dismantled the Iranian economy layer by layer. Support for Saddam Hussein during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, including the provision of chemical weapons precursors that killed tens of thousands of Iranians. The shooting down of Iran Air Flight 655 in 1988, which killed 290 civilian passengers, by a US Navy vessel that was never held accountable and whose captain was awarded a medal.

Iran never forgot any of it. And Iran's pursuit of nuclear capability, which began in earnest in the late 1980s, was inseparable from this history. A country that watched Iraq use chemical weapons against it, that watched America support the aggressor, and that watched Israel accumulate an undeclared nuclear arsenal of approximately 90 warheads with complete Western complicity, drew the entirely rational conclusion that the only guarantee of regime survival was nuclear deterrence.

This is the context that Western media almost never provides.

PART III: THE JCPOA, TRUMP'S WITHDRAWAL, AND THE DEATH OF DIPLOMACY

In 2015, after years of negotiations involving the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, Russia, and China, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action was signed. It was not a perfect agreement. But it was a functional one. Iran agreed to reduce its uranium stockpile by 98 percent, limit enrichment to 3.67 percent, reduce its centrifuges by two thirds, and allow intrusive IAEA inspections. In return, sanctions were lifted and Iran's frozen assets were released.

Every party to the agreement, every intelligence agency involved in its verification, and the IAEA itself confirmed Iran was complying with its terms.

In 2018, Donald Trump, under heavy lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, withdrew the United States from the JCPOA. The stated reason was that the deal was "defective." The actual reason, which is documented in the deliberations of Trump's own advisors at the time, was that Netanyahu had spent years making the destruction of Iranian nuclear capability the central strategic objective of his government, and Trump's circle was aligned with that objective.

When America withdrew, Iran had two choices. Accept a deal it had complied with while the other party had violated it, which was politically impossible domestically. Or begin rebuilding its nuclear program. It chose the latter, progressively and publicly.

By 2025, Iran had enriched uranium to 60 percent purity, short of the 90 percent weapons grade threshold but closer than at any previous point. It had approximately 400 kilograms of this material. It had a network of hardened, dispersed, underground facilities that made surgical destruction difficult. And critically, its relationship with Russia and China had deepened to the point where it was no longer diplomatically isolated in the way previous sanctions regimes had assumed.

The failure to return to the JCPOA between 2021 and 2024, despite multiple rounds of negotiation, was not primarily Iran's fault. The Biden administration, paralyzed by domestic political considerations and by Israeli and Gulf state lobbying, was unable to offer Iran the sanctions relief it had been promised and was owed under the original agreement. Iran's demands were not unreasonable. Its insistence on guarantees that the next American administration would not simply tear up any new agreement, as Trump had torn up the last one, was a rational response to documented American unreliability.

Nobody on cable news is telling you this. They are telling you Iran was the problem. The history says the picture is considerably more complicated.

PART IV: FEBRUARY 28, 2026 — THE NIGHT EVERYTHING CHANGED

In the predawn hours of February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched nearly 900 strikes in 12 hours targeting Iranian missiles, air defenses, military infrastructure, and leadership. The initial wave of strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of other officials, but it also killed approximately 170 people when a missile struck a girls' school adjacent to a naval base.

Read that sentence again. 170 people killed when a missile struck a girls' school. This fact received approximately 48 hours of media attention before being buried under the logistics of the ceasefire negotiations that followed.

The conflict followed the failure of indirect talks between the US and Iran, which themselves followed the October 2025 triggering of snapback sanctions against Iran under the 2015 nuclear deal by the UK, Germany, and France.

The snapback mechanism restored all UN sanctions on Iran, which had been suspended under the JCPOA. It was triggered because Iran had not returned to compliance with the nuclear deal. Iran had not returned to compliance because America had violated the deal first in 2018. The diplomatic logic is circular, and the person who pays is always the civilian in the girls' school.

Given Iran's weakened position following the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, years of sanctions, destabilizing protests, and the diminished position of Iran's allies during the Israel-Hamas war, the United States and Israel calculated that they had a greater opportunity to advance their objectives through military means than by diplomatic means.

This is the sentence that matters. Not nuclear danger. Not an imminent threat. A calculated decision that Iran was weak enough to hit. That is what started this war.

PART V: WHAT THE WAR ACTUALLY DID

The strikes of February 28 killed Khamenei and senior IRGC commanders. They damaged nuclear facilities significantly, though assessments of how much damage varied wildly between CIA Director John Ratcliffe's optimistic claims and independent analysis suggesting setbacks of months rather than years.

What they did not do was destroy Iran's will or its capability to respond.

The opening salvo triggered a torrent of hundreds of retaliatory missiles and thousands of drones from Iran across the region. Iranian ballistic missiles struck American bases in Qatar, Bahrain, and the UAE. Iranian attack drones targeted oil infrastructure across the Gulf. And most consequentially for the world economy, the IRGC closed the Strait of Hormuz, the 34 kilometer wide passage between Iran and Oman through which approximately 20 million barrels of oil per day, roughly 20 percent of global seaborne oil, transits daily.

The closure of the strait was not a tactical inconvenience. It was the most significant disruption to global energy supply in recorded history.

Brent crude rose to $106 per barrel, up more than 40 percent from $72 per barrel on February 27. LNG prices rose by almost 60 percent since the start of the war. The disruption led to global oil prices rising and caused fuel shortages in countries which imported most of their fuel from the Persian Gulf region. The impacts of the conflict were similar to the 1970s energy crisis, including acute supply shortages, currency volatility, inflation, and heightened risks of stagflation and recession.

In 2024, around 84 percent of the crude oil and 83 percent of the LNG passing through the Strait went to Asia; nearly 70 percent of the oil went to China, India, Japan, and South Korea. The countries suffering most acutely from an American war they had no vote in starting were Asian nations that had nothing to do with Iran's nuclear program.

Bangladesh was among the worst hit economies and is projected to have severe impacts on GDP growth inducing recession-like conditions. Bangladesh. A country with a GDP per capita of approximately $2,500, suffering recession conditions because Washington and Tel Aviv decided February 2026 was the moment to strike Iran.

The International Energy Agency called the Iran war the greatest global energy security challenge in history by May, with oil prices heading swiftly towards $5.00 per gallon.

There is one more fact from the economic wreckage that deserves its own paragraph. A Financial Times investigation found that $580 million bets on falling oil prices had been placed in the stock market by selling futures just 15 minutes before Donald Trump published his statement on postponing attacks on Iran for talks on March 23, 2026, which caused oil prices to fall for a while.

Someone knew the statement was coming before the market did. Someone made $580 million on that knowledge. This has received almost no sustained investigative attention from mainstream media.

PART VI: THE CEASEFIRE THAT IS NOT A CEASEFIRE

In April 2026, after five weeks of fighting, a ceasefire was announced. It lasted hours before Israel began striking Lebanon again.

This is the piece of the story that is being systematically obscured in Western media coverage. The ceasefire between the US and Iran has been continuously undermined by Israeli military operations in Lebanon, which Iran has made a condition for the deal's survival.

When Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a ceasefire that explicitly included Lebanon, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected that inclusion, asserting that the ceasefire did not include Lebanon, an assertion backed by Trump and Vance. Hezbollah said that it had halted its attacks. A few hours later Israel launched the strongest wave of attacks on Lebanon since the start of the war.

So the sequence was: ceasefire announced, Hezbollah stops, Israel attacks Lebanon, Iran closes the Strait again. Then repeat. For months.

The Lebanese government publicly condemned Hezbollah's renewed strikes against Israel for endangering and undermining the Lebanese state. It moved to ban Hezbollah's military activities, called on the group to place its weapons under government control, and end unauthorized attacks from Lebanese territory. The Lebanese government also condemned Israel's planned occupation and attacks on civilians.

Lebanon's own government condemned both parties. That is how you know the situation is beyond what any simple narrative can contain.

The war has precipitated a still-developing humanitarian crisis, resulted in deaths of more than 4,000 people from Israeli strikes in Lebanon, seen the forced displacement of over 1 million people, constituting more than 20 percent of Lebanon's population, and entailed the deployment of materiel and tactics that potentially constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity.

Over one million people, one fifth of Lebanon's entire population, displaced. This is happening right now. Today. While the news is discussing the terms of a deal that keeps collapsing.

PART VII: THE MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY SAYS

On June 17, 2026, Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding. Trump celebrated it on social media. The coverage was triumphant. Deal reached. War over. Strait opening.

Here is what the MOU actually contains and, more importantly, what it does not.

The agreement extends the current ceasefire for 60 days. The fate of Iran's nuclear program will be negotiated but remains unresolved for now. Trump made no mention of the nuclear issue in his initial posts, though this is the main reason he cited for launching the war in February.

Read that again. The stated reason for the war remains unresolved in the agreement that is being celebrated as ending the war.

The deal on the table includes Iran's commitment to halt enrichment and dismantle its nuclear sites, but the length of the pause is a point of disagreement. The United States is reportedly pushing for twenty years, while Iran reportedly will not go above ten, and the final terms will have to be negotiated during the 60-day pause.

Iran still has approximately 400 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium. Trump vowed to remove that nuclear material from the country but Tehran has not acquiesced to that demand, though it has agreed to talk.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has signaled that he does not feel bound by the agreement between Washington and Tehran and has no intention of withdrawing his forces from Lebanon.

Netanyahu is not bound by the deal his closest ally just signed. He has said so publicly. His defense minister has said Israel will keep troops in southern Lebanon indefinitely. And as of June 26, Trump confirmed that the US military struck Iranian missile and drone storage locations and coastal radar sites for violating the ceasefire agreement, after Iran fired drones at a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz.

The ceasefire is being violated by all parties, continuously, while being celebrated as a diplomatic achievement.

PART VIII: WHAT NOBODY IS SAYING ABOUT WHO BENEFITS

Every war has beneficiaries. The Iran war is no exception and identifying who has gained from it explains more about why it happened than any official justification.

The United States' domestic oil and gas industry has gained enormously. An analysis by the New York Times found that the biggest beneficiaries of the market changes were the United States, which saw an increase in exports and a revenue increase of about $50 billion, and Russia, which had steady exports and an increase of more than $15 billion in revenue, while all Persian Gulf nations showed declines.

America went to war against Iran. America's oil industry made $50 billion in additional revenue from that war. Russia, which is sanctioned by America and fighting America's partner Ukraine, made $15 billion. The Gulf states that host American military bases suffered economic losses. Process this.

Netanyahu considers Iran an existential threat and the deal is a major blow for Israel specifically, as it did not achieve the complete dismantlement of Iranian nuclear capability or regime change. Yet Israel has used this entire period to conduct extensive military operations in Lebanon with Western acquiescence, eliminating Hezbollah's military infrastructure in ways it could never have accomplished without the umbrella of a larger regional war.

A report from May 29 suggested that Netanyahu and his inner political circle were privately disgruntled with Trump over his alleged subversions and cancellations of Israeli plans to topple the Iranian government, and viewed the concept of an emerging American agreement with Iran as disastrous.

Netanyahu wanted the war to go further. He wanted regime change. Trump, facing congressional midterm elections in November 2026 and a domestic economy shaken by oil price inflation, decided a deal was more useful than a destroyed Iran. These two objectives are now openly in tension, with Israel continuing military operations that keep undermining the ceasefire that Trump needs for his domestic political purposes.

PART IX: IRAN'S INTERNAL COLLAPSE AND WHAT IT MEANS

The war has done something that decades of sanctions could not fully accomplish. It has brought Iran to the edge of internal fracture.

In the aftermath of the 12-day war of 2025, Iran's currency entered freefall, exacerbated by the imposition of new international sanctions in September. The economic spiral led to the outbreak of protests on December 28, 2025, which spread across Iran in January 2026. On January 8, security forces unleashed a brutal crackdown, killing at least 30,000 people according to officials in Iran's Ministry of Health.

30,000 people killed by their own government in a crackdown on protests. This happened in January 2026. It received significant coverage at the time and has been largely forgotten in the noise of ceasefire negotiations.

In a government poll as of June 20, 2026, nearly 60 percent of Iranians reported they were unable to continue with their lives financially, and 70 percent of the population demanded government changes.

Seventy percent of Iranians want government changes. This is not a population rallying around its leadership in the face of foreign aggression. This is a population that has been economically destroyed by a combination of its own government's choices and decades of external sanctions, and is telling pollsters it wants something different.

The Iranian regime that signed the MOU on June 17 is not the same Iran that existed in 2020. It is a government that has lost its Supreme Leader to American bombs, lost 30,000 of its citizens to its own crackdown, lost the economic confidence of 70 percent of its population, and is now negotiating from a position of fundamental weakness while trying to maintain the appearance of sovereignty.

PART X: THE 60-DAY WINDOW AND WHAT HAPPENS IF IT FAILS

The memorandum of understanding gives 60 days to negotiate a final agreement. The 60 days are running now.

The issues that need to be resolved in those 60 days are the same issues that have prevented agreement for the past decade:

Iran's nuclear enrichment rights, which it insists it has under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty it has been party to since 1970, and which the US insists must be zeroed out entirely. The fate of Iran's ballistic missile program. The removal of American sanctions, which Iran demands be comprehensive and verified before it takes any irreversible nuclear steps. The status of Iran's allies, particularly Hezbollah in Lebanon, which the US and Israel demand Iran stop supporting entirely. And the status of Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran considers its territorial water and the US considers international passage.

None of these questions have an easy answer. None of them were resolved in the MOU. The current agreement only gestures at these questions, leaving the substance for later, which is precisely where deals of this kind tend to come apart.

Trump told the New York Times that if no deal was reached, he could relaunch attacks on Iran or make the US the guardian of the Middle East in return for 20 percent of the region's revenues.

Twenty percent of the Middle East's revenues. The American president told the New York Times he wants a 20 percent cut of the Middle East's oil wealth as an alternative to a deal. This is not diplomacy. This is extortion dressed in diplomatic language and it is being reported as normal statecraft.

And as of June 27, Trump wrote on Truth Social: "There may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable, and will be forced to militarily complete the job that we very successfully started. If that happens, the Islamic Republic of Iran will no longer exist."

The president of the United States threatened the complete annihilation of a nation of 90 million people. Yesterday. This sentence appeared in the news and was scrolled past by millions of people who have been so normalized to extreme language that it no longer registers as what it is.

PART XI: THE BIGGER PICTURE NOBODY IS DRAWING

Step back from the daily ceasefire violations and the negotiating positions and the oil price updates. Look at the architecture of what has actually happened.

A country was struck because it was pursuing nuclear capability. That country was pursuing nuclear capability because its neighbor has undeclared nuclear weapons and because America destroyed the deal that would have prevented this outcome. The war has killed thousands of people, displaced over a million, destroyed Iran's economy, and sent global energy costs into crisis levels that are pushing Bangladesh toward recession and emptying petrol stations in Vietnam. The ceasefire being celebrated as a resolution leaves every core issue unresolved. The country most responsible for undermining the ceasefire, Israel, is operating with American protection while simultaneously being described by Trump as outside the terms of the deal. And the man who started the war is threatening to end the civilization of the country he is simultaneously negotiating with.

This is not a conflict about nuclear nonproliferation. It is a conflict about who controls the Middle East, who controls its energy architecture, and who has the right to determine what kinds of governments are permissible in the region.

Iran made a choice in 1979 to be independent of the American-led order. Every major development since has been, at its root, a consequence of that choice and America's refusal to accept it.

The deal being negotiated right now will not resolve that fundamental tension. It will paper over it for however long the 60 days produce, and then the underlying reality will reassert itself.

CONCLUSION: WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY BE WATCHING

Do not watch the ceasefire announcements. Watch whether Israel withdraws from Lebanon. It will not, and every day it does not is another day the ceasefire with Iran erodes.

Do not watch Trump's social media posts about the deal. Watch the IAEA's access to Iranian nuclear sites. The IAEA has not been granted access to bombed enrichment sites targeted by the US. Without verification, any nuclear agreement is a press release.

Do not watch the oil price headlines. Watch the 60 day negotiating deadline and whether the core issues, enrichment, sanctions, missiles, proxies, get resolved or get deferred again.

Do not watch the coverage that frames this as a story about Iran's nuclear threat. Watch the fact that Israel has an undeclared nuclear arsenal of approximately 90 warheads and has never been asked to sign the Non Proliferation Treaty and has never faced a single sanction or military threat over it. The selective application of non-proliferation norms is not non-proliferation. It is geopolitics using non-proliferation as a costume.

And watch this: 70 percent of Iranians want government change. That population has now been through a war, a brutal crackdown, economic freefall, and a signing ceremony that their own government described as a victory while most of them cannot pay for food. What happens inside Iran over the next 12 months may matter more than anything the negotiators in Switzerland agree to.

The war is not over. The deal is not done. The ceasefire is being violated as you read this. And the news is already moving on to the next thing.

You should not.
